newsitem.title: USA: PECO chairman confident of dividend.
newsitem.headline: PECO chairman confident of dividend.

text.p: PECO Energy Co said Tuesday Chairman Joseph F. Paquette Jr is confident the company can maintain its quarterly dividend.
The company said he released a statement about the dividend in response to concerns expressed this week about the utility's ability to maintain its current annual dividend rate of $1.80 per share.
These concerns have "caused the market price of the company's stock to decrease approximately $3 per share over the last 24 hours," the company said.
In afternoon trading, the stock was off 1-1/2 at 22-1/2.
By midafternoon, nearly 3 million shares had changed hands.

"I want our shareholders to know that I am confident that we can maintain the current dividend of $1.80 per share for the foreseeable future. Although the electric utility industry is faced with the challenge of transitioning to a competitive market, I am optimistic that the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission will reach a just and reasonable decision on our stranded costs which will enable the Company to maintain its financial condition."
In October, PECO declared a quarterly payment of $0.45 per share, raising its dividend from the $0.435 it had been paying. Monday, directors again declared a $0.45 payment.

Earlier Tuesday, the utility's common stock was downgraded by Merrill Lynch and Oppenheimer, which said the consensus earnings estimate of $2.60 per share for 1997 was too high and projected the company would earn $2.10.

Monday, PECO reported 1996 earnings of $2.24 per share, down from $2.64 in 1995, saying the decrease was primarily attributable to increased costs associated with the shutdown of Salem Generating Station Units No. 1 and No. 2.
The nuclear power plant, located in southern New Jersey, is operated by Public Service Enterprise Group Inc. Both PECO and PSE&G have a 42.59 percent interest in the plant.

PECO also cited lower electric revenues from retail sales resulting from unfavorable weather conditions, the gain on the 1995 sale of Conowingo Power Co, higher customer expenses, and accelerated depreciation of its investment in the Limerick nuclear power plant and other assets.

These decreases were partially offset by improvements in operating and maintenance costs; savings from the Company's ongoing debt and preferred stock refunding program; and higher electric revenues from sales to other utilities.
Record levels of electric sales were achieved last year, increasing 11.5 percent from 1995 due primarily to the increased sales to other utilities.
In the fourth quarter, electric sales increased 9 percent as compared to the prior fourth quarter primarily due to increased sales to other utilities.
Last week the utility put its potential stranded assets at $7.1 billion when it announced plans to refinance these costs under a new Pennsylvania law. ((-- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710.))
